extracted.intended_audience: NIH extramural investigators (PIs) preparing or reviewing competing continuation/renewal (RPG) applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how NIH competing continuation (renewal) applications are — and should be — reviewed, with emphasis on productivity, alignment to prior aims/goals, and contextual factors that affect renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glamour/major-impact publications (Did you knock our socks off?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary, high-impact findings or 'GlamourPub' level publications that visibly change a field or are seen as major advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have truly spectacular findings/publications, reviewers will often give strong credit even if other items (e.g., exact alignment with prior Aims or IC mission) are lacking. Consider whether 'GlamMag' work substitutes for attention to originally proposed experiments; in some cases spectacular output can outweigh mismatches, though panels may still debate relevance to the funder's mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raw productivity (Were you productive?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of publications produced during the prior interval of support; more papers generally improves a renewal's reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers look favorably on being 'fabulously productive' or meeting subfield norms; modest productivity that meets peers' standards is creditworthy. Use field norms (e.g., papers per grant-dollar benchmarks) to set expectations, but be mindful of attribution issues when multiple grants exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality/impact of publications (real scientific progress vs paper count)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive contribution of the publications — whether they represent 'real scientific progress' rather than merely adding to the publication count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels may debate quality vs quantity: well-done, impactful papers can matter more than many low-impact ones. Clarify significance in the Progress Report to help reviewers judge impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity aligned with overall programmatic goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work published under the prior award addresses the broad theme or 'big idea' described in the original application (what was in the first sentences of the Specific Aims page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal applicants should explicitly tell reviewers in the Progress Report how prior outputs relate to overarching goals, because reviewers do not have the full prior application. If publications relate to the general theme, reviewers will view this positively even if exact original Aims were not followed to the letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing original Specific Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the prior project completed or advanced the Specific Aims proposed in the awarded application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some reviewers obsess over matching each Aim; others accept natural changes in direction. Applicants should document which Aims were addressed with published data or preliminary data. Reviewers must balance expectation of following Aims against legitimate scientific shifts (scooping, new directions, failed predictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of preliminary data/published data demonstrating Aim completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of published papers or ready-to-submit Preliminary Data in the renewal application that show the prior work accomplished the proposed experiments/Aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing clear evidence (publications or preliminary data) that link to the proposed Aims strengthens the renewal. Even modest journals' papers tied to Aims can credit a renewal if documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to prior reviewers' critiques (controls/additional experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether suggested controls or key additional experiments noted in the prior summary statement were performed or otherwise addressed in subsequent work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may penalize renewals that ignore prior reviewer's suggested crucial experiments. Applicants should describe how prior criticisms were handled (done, partially done, or why not feasible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of publications to specific grants (multi-award attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: How publications are attributed when PIs have multiple awards, and whether reviewers consider per-grant productivity meaningful given shared attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels often dispute whether publications truly arose from the specific prior award; multiple grants dilute per-grant productivity metrics. Applicants should clearly state contributions supported by the award. Reviewers should be aware of system-wide attribution issues that can advantage multi-award PIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of the prior summary statement/score
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that reviewers of the renewal can see the prior Summary Statement, score and percentile, which may influence attitudes toward the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may be biased (positively or negatively) by the prior score/percentile; the post questions whether that should affect evaluation. Applicants cannot hide prior scores; reviewers should consciously separate past critique from current accomplishments where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and realistic publication pipeline constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The real-world timeline between funding, data collection, manuscript preparation, submission, review, revision and acceptance — e.g., limited months between renewal submission and project end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should account for realistic constraints (new PIs, slow human/longitudinal studies, breeding timelines) when judging productivity. Applicants should document project timelines and explain why fewer publications may nonetheless represent substantial progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study-section/field culture and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Norms in a given study section (long-running thematic grants vs project-style grants) shape expectations for what counts as renewal-appropriate productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different panels expect different evidence (long-term payoff vs project-complete papers). Applicants should understand their study section culture and present Progress Reports accordingly; reviewers should assess within cultural norms of their field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to the funding IC's mission/programmatic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work produced under the award bears on the mission of the funding Institute/Center (IC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-profile work that is not closely related to the IC's mission may be viewed unfavorably for renewal; applicants should justify relevance or consider submitting a new grant if the direction diverged. Reviewers should consider mission alignment as part of relevance evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-through credit (finishing promised work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit given for 'follow through' — actually completing work that was proposed and demonstrating that the lab delivered on plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and panels value applicants who follow through on proposed projects; however, this is not universally rewarded. Applicants should highlight completed aims and tie outputs to prior commitments to earn this credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in the Progress Report (list of publications and explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The renewal application must include a list of publications resulting from the prior award and a Progress Report overviewing accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, explicit reporting (which papers resulted from the award, how they connect to aims/theme, which experiments were completed or dropped, and reasons) helps reviewers judge productivity and relevance. Lack of clarity invites unfavorable debate.
